Share this article paywall-free Email Copy Link MARIETTA — Thousands of Lockheed Martin employees gathered at the Marietta plant Thursday to commemorate 70 years since the first flight of the C-130 Hercules.On Aug. 23, 1954, the YC-130 prototype’s first flight took place at Lockheed’s Burbank, California, plant.Since then, every production of the four-engine turboprop military transport aircraft has been built at Lockheed’s Marietta production facility, making it the longest running military aircraft production program in history.There have been over 2,700 C-130s delivered to 70 global operators across 6 continents, logging over 24 million flight hours.“You can’t say C-130 without saying Marietta. It’s one in the same,” said Jamie Holdaway, a Lockheed flight engineer and loadmaster.Holdaway was recognized during the celebration for having logged 10,000 hours on the aircraft — a total of 416 days. That time has been spent involved in many of the Hercules’ mission capabilities, including air and ground refueling, disaster relief and humanitarian aid.Holdaway, as well as Rod McLean, general manager of Lockheed’s Marietta site, believe the aircraft is an integral part of Cobb County.“(This anniversary) signifies how Lockheed Martin is one of the key cornerstones of Cobb County and the metro Atlanta region’s economy,” McLean said. “We’ve delivered an economic impact of significant value that created high-paying jobs for the Cobb County area.”About 5,600 people are currently employed at the Marietta location, many of whom are local residents.Four employees were honored during the celebration for their more than 60 years of service on the C-130 program: Flight line/test mechanic Joe Yeargin, jig and fixture builder Harold Taylor, machinist general Ray Touchton and project management representative Mel Woods.During his speech, Greg Ulmer, president of Lockheed Martin Aeronautics, said the event was just as much a celebration of those involved with the C-130 as it was about the aircraft itself.“That’s your blood, sweat and tears in everything we do in that machine,” Ulmer said. “When each new C-130J rolls off the line, it’s a culmination of dedication and hard work from a great number of teammates.”Ulmer began working at the plant as a flight test engineer about a year before the first flight of the C-130J model in 1996.Function over FashionThe C-130J is the latest addition to the C-130 fleet and is considered “the most advanced Hercules ever built,” according to Lockheed.The aircraft was introduced in 1999. Since then, more than 545 C-130Js have been built and delivered to 26 operators across 22 countries. Over 3 million flight hours have been logged from the newest version of the plane, known as the Super Hercules.McLean said C-130 production has always prioritized function over fashion.“While the C-130 may look the same from the outside, there’s been quite a few modernization improvements and structural enhancements that allow the aircraft to fly longer,” McLean said.New digital flight control computers allow the aircraft to operate more effectively with a smaller crew size, added McLean.According to Lockheed, the C-130J is the only tactical-by-design medium-sized airlift that meets all of the requirements of the tactical airlift mission. It has 19 mission capabilities, ranging from intelligence and reconnaissance to firefighting and search and rescue operations.The C-130J sits 38 feet 10 inches tall, has a wingspan of 132 feet seven inches long, and at a maximum payload of 42,000 pounds, has a range of 2,071 miles, according to the U.S. Air Force.Powered by four Rolls-Royce turboprop engines that produce 4,700 horsepower each, the plane can travel up to 417 miles per hour at 22,000 feet.At the back is a large loading ramp and door which allows the plane to carry oversized cargo, including armored vehicles, and allows the plane to be used in an aerial delivery role, where loads up to 42,000 pounds can be dropped from the air.In celebration of decades of Hercules missions, several attendees shared their experiences working on the aircraft.Air Force Lt. Col. Kyle Gauthier has logged over 3,000 flight hours on the C-130J.In his speech, Gauthier shared memories from traveling the world on the aircraft from doing airdrops over the Central African Republic to feeding tigers by hand at a local zoo in Entebbe, Uganda.Gauthier added that, in his opinion, the C-130Js most significant mission is aeromedical evacuation and its ability to bring personnel to safety.“With this plane, we can land at 3,000 feet and take off from the same distance which enables us to bring anything we need closer,” Gauthier said.Bill “Shaggy” Andrews, Lockheed Martin vice president of air mobility and maritime missions domestic programs, shared that his experiences on C-130, specifically while stationed at Aviano Air Base in Italy during the Bosnian war, showed him just how important the people behind the scenes were.“We depended on the airplane and the airplane was reliable because you all made that happen,” Andrews said to the crowd. “What we did as a crew, none of that would have happened without the (almost) 6,000 people here to continue to pump these Hercs out every day.”Looking ForwardThis year, the Marietta plant will produce about 20 C-130Js. Just a few weeks ago, New Zealand received their first Super Hercules, said Ulmer.Ulmer added that each delivery represents something different for each customer and their citizens.For some, it means better life saving mission capabilities.“For the U.S. Air Force, the Super Hercules provides weather reconnaissance data to prepare for hurricanes or tropical storms. For people across the Indo-Pacific, the sight of a J during the holidays means Operation Christmas Drop with food, school books, toys (and) medicine.”McLean said Lockheed Martin plans to sustain their production rate over the next several years, thanks to firm commitments that will drive production into the 2030s.“I would have told you in 2010 that we wouldn’t be producing C-130Js in 2020, but we’re going to be producing C-130Js in 2035 and beyond,” Ulmer said.
